warmup.q: A checkout submits two tasks to newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() inside try-with-resources. The bank task takes 2 s. The stock task throws after 100 ms. The checkout calls stock.get() first. When does its exception reach the caller?
options: After about 100 ms: stock.get() throws, and the executor cancels the bank task
After about 2 s: stock.get() throws at 100 ms, but close() waits for the bank task to finish
Never: the executor logs the stock task's exception and returns null
After about 100 ms, and the bank task is still running when the caller sees the exception
warmup.why: get() throws at 100 ms, but leaving the try block runs close(), which waits for every task. Nothing cancels the bank task, so the failed checkout still takes 2 s. The last option is what happens with a long-lived executor kept in a field: the method fails fast, and the bank task keeps running with nobody waiting for it. The first section runs both.

opening:
Picture a big table at the restaurant, looked after by a head waiter. The table orders, and he sends three helpers at once: one to the kitchen for the soup, one to the bar for the drinks, one to the cellar for a bottle of wine. Then he stays at the table until all three are back, so nobody is forgotten.

Now the cellar is out of that wine, and its helper comes straight back. The table changes its order. A careful head waiter calls the other two helpers back at once. A careless one lets them carry on, and a soup arrives for an order that no longer exists.

Lesson 3's fan-out is the careless head waiter. It waits for every helper, which looks complete, so the trap is easy to miss. But when one helper fails, nothing calls the others back. Lesson 4 left a second gap: a ThreadLocal doesn't follow the work into the helpers.

In this lesson, we'll watch a failed checkout keep working, build a scope that calls the helpers back, meet the JDK's own scope and pin a note to the order. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a head waiter who sends helpers and stays at the table until they're back. The executor fan-out stayed too, but it never called anyone back, so a sold-out checkout still waited two seconds for the bank. A scope adds the missing rule: the first failure cancels the rest, and nothing outlives the block. A scoped value is the note pinned to the order.

Now search your own code for a list of Futures, and check what happens to the others when one get() throws.

Next, we'll move a whole service to virtual threads. Its old pool of 10 threads also kept a limit that nobody wrote down. Which limit, and how do we write it back?

sections.h: A failed checkout keeps working: what an executor fan-out leaves out
sections.html:
Let's set up the example first. A fan-out, from lesson 3 of this track, starts several calls at once and then collects all their answers. Each call is a subtask: a piece of a bigger job that runs on a thread of its own, here a virtual thread, the cheap kind the JDK sets aside whenever it waits. To save time, the shop's checkout now asks two services at the same moment instead of one after the other. The stock service says whether the items are in the warehouse, and the bank says whether the payment is approved. If the items are sold out, the bank's answer is useless.

Here is that fan-out in the lesson 3 shape. An executor is an object that runs tasks for you, and submit hands back a Future, a handle on a result that arrives later:

Java
try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<Approval> bank = perTask.submit(() -> theBank.approve(order));    // 2 s on a bad day
    Future<Stock> stock = perTask.submit(() -> stockService.check(order));   // fails at 100 ms: sold out
    return new Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get());
}
Kotlin
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask ->
    val bank = perTask.submit(Callable { theBank.approve(order) })     // 2 s on a bad day
    val stock = perTask.submit(Callable { stockService.check(order) }) // fails at 100 ms: sold out
    Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get())
}

Predict when the checkout fails. The stock service says "sold out" after 100 ms, so a careful program would give up at 100 ms. LeakDemo, in the Try it below, runs this exact shape as variant A:

A: an executor per checkout, closed by try-with-resources
  2,027 ms  bank: answered, but nobody needs the answer
  2,069 ms  checkout failed: stock service: sold out

The checkout was doomed at 100 ms, and it failed at 2 seconds. stock.get() threw at 100 ms, as it should. But leaving the try block runs close(), which waits for every task, and nothing told the bank call to stop. The bank, true to form, took its full two seconds to answer a question nobody was asking any more.

Many programs keep one long-lived executor in a field instead. LeakDemo tries that too, as variant B:

B: one shared executor
    102 ms  checkout failed: stock service: sold out
  2,001 ms  bank: answered, but nobody needs the answer

Now the checkout fails fast, at 102 ms. But the bank call runs on for another two seconds, for a checkout that is long gone. It's the helper still in the cellar, fetching wine for a table that has left. A call like that holds a connection, and maybe a permit from lesson 3's semaphore. Under load these orphans pile up, and nothing in a thread dump, the list of every thread a program has, says which checkout they belonged to.

Three things are missing, and they are the same three in every fan-out:

  • A failure cancels nothing. To stop the others, you'd call cancel(true) on each future, in every fan-out, on every error path.
  • The subtasks' lives aren't tied to the code. A Future is a value you can store anywhere, so nothing promises that the threads a method started have ended when it returns.
  • The order's details don't follow the work. A ThreadLocal is a variable with a separate value for each thread, so one set by the checkout, such as the order id for the log, is empty in the subtasks.

Structured concurrency fixes the first two with one rule: a subtask can't outlive the block of code that started it, just as a local variable can't outlive its method. Scoped values, at the end of this lesson, fix the third.

Waiting for every subtask is half the job. When one fails, the others must stop too.

So we need a head waiter who calls the helpers back. Let's build one.

try.title: Watch the orphaned call
steps: Read LeakDemo. Variant A opens an executor per checkout in try-with-resources. Variant B uses one shared executor. For each, predict when the checkout fails and whether the bank call finishes.
Run it with the command below.
Fix variant A by hand. Wrap stock.get() in a try, call bank.cancel(true) in the catch (ExecutionException e), then rethrow e. Run it again.

code.title: LeakDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** * A checkout asks two services at the same time: the bank, which takes 2 s on a bad day, * and the stock service, which says "sold out" after 100 ms. Once the stock check has failed, * the bank's answer is useless. Watch what happens to the bank call anyway. */ public class LeakDemo { static volatile long t0; static void log(String what) { System.out.printf("%,7d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what); } static String bank() throws InterruptedException { try { Thread.sleep(2_000); // the bank, on a bad day log("bank: answered, but nobody needs the answer"); return "approved"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("bank: interrupted, stopped early"); throw e; } } static String stock() throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(100); throw new IllegalStateException("stock service: sold out"); } // A: an executor per checkout, in try-with-resources static String checkoutA() throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> bank = perTask.submit(LeakDemo::bank); Future<String> stock = perTask.submit(LeakDemo::stock); return stock.get() + " " + bank.get(); // throws at 100 ms... } // ...but close() waits for the bank } static final ExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // B: one long-lived executor for the whole shop static String checkoutB() throws Exception { Future<String> bank = SHARED.submit(LeakDemo::bank); Future<String> stock = SHARED.submit(LeakDemo::stock); return stock.get() + " " + bank.get(); // throws at 100 ms, and returns } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("A: an executor per checkout, closed by try-with-resources"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { checkoutA(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("checkout failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } System.out.println("B: one shared executor"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { checkoutB(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("checkout failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } Thread.sleep(2_500); // stay alive to see what B left behind SHARED.close(); } }

Once the stock check has failed, * the bank's answer is useless. Watch what happens to the bank call anyway. */ @Volatile private var t0 = 0L private fun log(what: String) = println("%,7d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what)) private fun bank(): String = try { Thread.sleep(2_000) // the bank, on a bad day log("bank: answered, but nobody needs the answer") "approved" } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("bank: interrupted, stopped early") throw e } private fun stock(): String { Thread.sleep(100) throw IllegalStateException("stock service: sold out") } // A: an executor per checkout, closed by use {} private fun checkoutA(): String = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val bank = perTask.submit(Callable { bank() }) val stock = perTask.submit(Callable { stock() }) stock.get() + " " + bank.get() // throws at 100 ms... } // ...but close() waits for the bank private val shared = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() // B: one long-lived executor for the whole shop private fun checkoutB(): String { val bank = shared.submit(Callable { bank() }) val stock = shared.submit(Callable { stock() }) return stock.get() + " " + bank.get() // throws at 100 ms, and returns } fun main() { println("A: an executor per checkout, closed by use {}") t0 = System.nanoTime() try { checkoutA() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { log("checkout failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } println("B: one shared executor") t0 = System.nanoTime() try { checkoutB() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { log("checkout failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } Thread.sleep(2_500) // stay alive to see what B left behind shared.close() }

try.expect: A: the bank call finishes at about 2,000 ms, and only then does the checkout fail, although the answer was known at 100 ms (2,027 and 2,069 ms in a run here). B: the checkout fails at about 100 ms (102 ms here), and the bank call still finishes at about 2,000 ms, for a checkout that is long gone. After your fix, A prints bank: interrupted, stopped early and fails at about 100 ms (128 ms here). That fixes one fan-out. Every other fan-out in the program needs the same code on every error path.

sections.h: The head waiter: a scope that owns its subtasks
sections.html:
Here is the head waiter again, part by part. He is the scope: an object that starts subtasks and owns them. Sending a helper is fork, which starts a subtask on a new virtual thread. Waiting at the table is join, which waits for the subtasks. Calling the others back when one returns with bad news is fail fast: the first failure cancels the rest, and join reports it at once. And not leaving the table until every helper is back is close. When the block ends, every thread the scope started has ended, whether the block returned, threw or was interrupted.

In code the shape is always the same. Both versions use this lesson's lab class, FailFastScope, a small scope you build yourself on a plain executor:

Java
try (var scope = new FailFastScope()) {                                   // the head waiter
    Supplier<Approval> bank = scope.fork(() -> theBank.approve(order));
    Supplier<Stock> stock = scope.fork(() -> stockService.check(order));
    scope.join();                                                         // waits, or throws the first failure
    return new Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get());
}                                                                         // close(): no subtask is still running
Kotlin
FailFastScope().use { scope ->                                            // the head waiter
    val bank = scope.fork { theBank.approve(order) }
    val stock = scope.fork { stockService.check(order) }
    scope.join()                                                          // waits, or throws the first failure
    Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get())
}                                                                         // close(): no subtask is still running

Read it aloud: send two helpers, wait for both or for the first bad news, and don't leave until they're back. fork returns a handle, a Supplier whose get() gives the subtask's result after join.

Let's trace the smallest case, with the stock check failing and the bank slow:

  • At 0 ms, the scope forks both subtasks, each on a new virtual thread.
  • At 100 ms, the stock subtask throws. Its wrapper records the failure as the first one and cancels the scope.
  • Cancel means interrupt: a signal that wakes a waiting thread with an InterruptedException. The bank subtask, blocked in a network read, wakes up that way.
  • The bank subtask's failure arrives second, so it doesn't replace the first.
  • join() sees the first failure and throws it, at about 100 ms.
  • close() waits until the bank thread has really finished.
  • A subtask forked after the cancel never runs, and its handle throws if you ask for a result.

How does the lab do this? Each forked task runs inside a small wrapper. If the task throws, the wrapper records the failure with AtomicReference.compareAndSet(null, failure), read as "store it only if nobody stored one first", so exactly one failure wins. Then it calls shutdownNow() on the executor, which interrupts every running subtask and refuses new ones.

An interrupt stops code that waits in sleep, a network read, a lock or a queue, which covers almost all waiting on virtual threads. It doesn't stop a loop that computes and never checks the interrupt flag. In Java, cancelling is a request the code has to cooperate with. Here the head waiter picture breaks: a real helper hears his name called, but a subtask that never waits and never checks hears nothing.

One detail looks right and is wrong. You might cancel each sibling with future.cancel(true). That interrupts the thread, but it also marks the future as done at once. On JDK 21, newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor counts a task as finished as soon as its future is done. So close() can return while the cancelled task still runs its finally block, giving back a permit, say. shutdownNow() interrupts without touching the futures, so close() keeps waiting until each thread has truly ended. The lab's close() test catches exactly this bug, which is a good reason to prefer the JDK's own scope once you can use it.

A subtask must never outlive the block that forked it. Make the scope wait for threads, not for futures.

Check yourself: in your FailFastScope, the stock check fails at 100 ms. The bank call is blocked in a network read, and a third subtask runs a 3-second loop that computes and never checks the interrupt flag. When does join() throw, and when does close() return? join() throws at about 100 ms with the stock failure. close() returns at about 3 seconds: the interrupt stops the network read but not the loop, and close() waits for every thread.

We built a head waiter by hand. The JDK has one of its own, still a preview in JDK 25. Let's see what that means.

sections.h: StructuredTaskScope: the JDK's own scope, still a preview in JDK 25
sections.html:
StructuredTaskScope, in java.util.concurrent, is the JDK's scope. It's a preview API. An API is the set of classes and methods a library offers, and a preview one is finished and fully specified, and still allowed to change its mind in the next release. The compiler and the JVM refuse it unless you pass --enable-preview. Its current shape arrived in JDK 25 (JEP 505, the fifth preview). It stayed a preview in JDK 26 (JEP 525) and JDK 27 (JEP 533). JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28, due in March 2027, with the JDK 27 API unchanged. So the Gradle labs, which must run on JDK 21, leave it out, and this lesson's demo lives in labs/vthreads/preview/ as a single-file program for JDK 25.

Here is the checkout in the JDK 25 shape:

Java
Receipt checkout(Order order) throws InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {          // fail on the first failure
        Subtask<Approval> bank = scope.fork(() -> theBank.approve(order));
        Subtask<Stock> stock = scope.fork(() -> stockService.check(order));
        scope.join();               // JDK 25: throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException
        return new Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get());
    }                               // close(): cancels what is left and waits for it
}
Kotlin
fun checkout(order: Order): Receipt =
    StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope ->            // fail on the first failure
        val bank = scope.fork(Callable { theBank.approve(order) })
        val stock = scope.fork(Callable { stockService.check(order) })
        scope.join()               // JDK 25: throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException
        Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get())
    }                              // close(): cancels what is left and waits for it

It has the same shape as FailFastScope, with stricter rules. Subtasks run on virtual threads. Calling get() before join() throws IllegalStateException. Scopes must nest like blocks, and the JDK checks that you close them in that order. And a thread dump written as JSON, a structured text format (jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json threads.json), groups each scope's threads under it, so you can see which checkout a thread belongs to.

ScopeDemo, in the Try it below, is LeakDemo's checkout written this way. Predict the timeline first. On JDK 25, run from labs/, it printed:

$ java --enable-preview --source 25 vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java
    135 ms  [order-42] bank: interrupted, stopped early
    165 ms  [order-42] checkout failed: stock service: sold out
    165 ms  [-] done: the binding has ended, and no subtask is still running

That's the careful head waiter. The stock failure cancelled the bank call, join() threw at once, and nothing was still running when the block ended. The times are a little over 100 ms because the first run also loads the classes it needs. The [order-42] on each line comes from a scoped value, the topic of the next section.

Leave out the flag, and javac, the Java compiler, stops at the first line that uses the API: error: StructuredTaskScope is a preview API and is disabled by default. Kotlin's compiler doesn't check for preview APIs, and on JDK 25 the Kotlin jar even ran without the flag here. Don't lean on that: the API can change in the next JDK, flag or no flag.

The scope's policy is a joiner, an object you pass to open that decides when join() returns and what it gives back. JDK 25 has four built in:

  • Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), the default: fail fast, and join() returns null.
  • Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow(): fail fast, and join() returns the subtasks as a Stream<Subtask<T>>.
  • Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(): the first success wins, and the scope cancels the rest.
  • Joiner.awaitAll(): wait for everything and never throw. You check each subtask's state().

A second argument changes the scope's settings, such as a timeout. Here the shop asks two delivery companies for a price and takes whichever answers first:

Java
try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Price>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(),
        cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)))) {
    scope.fork(() -> fastPost.price(parcel));
    scope.fork(() -> cheapPost.price(parcel));
    return scope.join();        // the first price back; the slower call is cancelled
}
Kotlin
StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow<Price>()) { cf ->
    cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))
}.use { scope ->
    scope.fork(Callable { fastPost.price(parcel) })
    scope.fork(Callable { cheapPost.price(parcel) })
    scope.join()               // the first price back; the slower call is cancelled
}

If the 300 ms run out first, the scope cancels both calls, and join() throws StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException.

Expect small edits whenever you change JDKs, because that is what preview means. JDK 26 renamed anySuccessfulResultOrThrow to anySuccessfulOrThrow, and allSuccessfulOrThrow now returns a List of results. In JDK 27 the built-in joiners make join() throw the ordinary checked ExecutionException, like Future.get(), instead of FailedException. Your lab scope already behaves that way. And articles from the JDK 21 days show new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure() with throwIfFailed(). That API is gone, and it doesn't compile on JDK 25.

A preview API can change in the next release. Pin the JDK version, and keep preview code small and in one place.

The scope calls the helpers back. One gap from the first section is left: the order's own details, which a ThreadLocal failed to carry into the subtasks.

steps: This one needs JDK 25 exactly, because --enable-preview works only for the JDK's own release. Check with java -version. It runs outside Gradle, as a single-file program, from labs/.
Run ScopeDemo and compare its timeline with LeakDemo's. Look at the [order-42] on the bank's line: the subtask can read the checkout's scoped value.
Make stock() return "in stock" after its sleep instead of throwing. Predict how long the checkout takes, then run it.

Now open the scope with a timeout: StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))) (in Kotlin, open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow<Any>()) { cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) }). Predict, then run.

From labs/: // java --enable-preview --source 25 vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java // The checkout from LeakDemo, written with a scope. Not part of the Gradle build. import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope; import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner; // for the Try it import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Subtask; public class ScopeDemo { static final ScopedValue<String> ORDER_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String what) { System.out.printf("%,7d ms [%s] %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, ORDER_ID.orElse("-"), what); } static String bank() throws InterruptedException { try { Thread.sleep(2_000); // the bank, on a bad day log("bank: answered"); return "approved"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("bank: interrupted, stopped early"); throw e; } } static String stock() throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(100); throw new IllegalStateException("stock service: sold out"); } static String checkout() throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // default joiner: fail on the first failure Subtask<String> bank = scope.fork(ScopeDemo::bank); Subtask<String> stock = scope.fork(ScopeDemo::stock); scope.join(); // throws FailedException at about 100 ms return stock.get() + " " + bank.get(); } // close(): every subtask has ended } static void handle() { try { log("checkout: " + checkout()); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.FailedException e) { log("checkout failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException e) { log("checkout timed out"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { ScopedValue.where(ORDER_ID, "order-42").run(ScopeDemo::handle); // subtasks see order-42 too log("done: the binding has ended, and no subtask is still running"); } }

try.expect: First run: a little after 100 ms the bank's line says interrupted, stopped early, then checkout failed: stock service: sold out, then the done line with [-], because the binding has ended (135, 165 and 165 ms in a run here; the Kotlin jar printed 144, 172 and 173 ms). When both succeed, the checkout arrives after about 2,000 ms (2,078 ms here), since the default joiner waits for every subtask. With the 500 ms timeout, the bank is interrupted at about 500 ms and the checkout reports checkout timed out (551 ms here). In every case the done line comes last: the scope never leaves a subtask running.

sections.h: A note pinned to the order: scoped values replace request ThreadLocals
sections.html:
A checkout carries details that many methods need but few should have to pass along: the order id for the log, or the customer's name for the receipt. The usual tool has been a ThreadLocal, the apron pocket from lesson 4 of this track. For this job the pocket has three problems:

  • Anyone can write in it. Any code can call set(), so the code that reads the value can't tell where it came from.
  • Nobody empties it unless someone calls remove(). On a pooled thread, a value one task forgot is still there for the next.
  • Its inheritance is a copy. An InheritableThreadLocal copies its values into every new thread, so that's one copy per subtask, and a later change in the parent never reaches the children.

ScopedValueDemo, in the Try it below, shows the second problem first. A task on a one-thread pool sets the customer to ann and forgets to remove it. Then the next task on the same thread asks who its customer is:

1. next task, same pool thread: ThreadLocal=ann, ScopedValue=unbound

That task never set anything, and it believes it's serving Ann. On a receipt, that's a stranger's name.

A scoped value is the replacement. Picture a note pinned to the order: everyone who works on the order can read it, nobody can change it, and it comes off when the order closes. In code, you bind a value for the length of one call. Everything that call runs can read it, and nobody can change it. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506), so they need no flag:

Java
static final ScopedValue<String> CUSTOMER = ScopedValue.newInstance();

void handle(Order order) {
    ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, order.customer()).run(() -> checkout(order));   // bound only inside run()
}

static String receiptLine(String item) {
    return item + " for " + CUSTOMER.get();     // NoSuchElementException if nobody bound it
}
Kotlin
val CUSTOMER: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance()

fun handle(order: Order) {
    ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, order.customer).run(Runnable { checkout(order) })   // bound only inside run()
}

fun receiptLine(item: String): String =
    item + " for " + CUSTOMER.get()              // NoSuchElementException if nobody bound it

Map it back to the note. Pinning the note is where(...), the order being open is the call inside run(), reading the note is get(), and the note comes off when run() returns. There is no set(). To use another value for a nested call, bind again with where(...).run(...), and the outer value comes back when that call returns. isBound() and orElse(...) let code handle the case where nothing is bound, and call(...) is the version that returns a value and may throw. The rest of the demo shows each rule:

2. inside run():   ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=ann
   after run():    ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=unbound
3. nested:         ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=ben
   outer again:    ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=ann
4. plain thread:   ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=unbound

The fourth line is the rule to remember. A scoped value flows into subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope, as [order-42] did in ScopeDemo. The child doesn't get a copy: it reads the parent's binding, which is safe because nobody can change the binding, and the scope ends before the binding does. A thread you start yourself, or an executor task, could outlive the binding, so it gets nothing. Pass the value as an argument there.

Here the note picture breaks a little. A paper note stays on the order for anyone who picks it up, even a helper borrowed from another table. A scoped value is visible only to code inside the call that bound it, and to that call's own scope.

On JDK 25 that gives a clear split. Use scoped values for new request details today, with no flag. Their flow into subtasks needs StructuredTaskScope, which is still a preview. Keep ThreadLocal where a library requires it, and clear it in a finally.

Details that belong to one call should live as long as that call. Bind them with a scoped value, and let nobody change them.

In the lab you build the head waiter itself: FailFastScope, on a plain executor, with JDK 21 APIs only.

try.title: ThreadLocal and ScopedValue side by side
steps: You need JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final there, so this runs without --enable-preview.
Read ScopedValueDemo and predict its six lines of output before you run it.
Run it. Then, in part 1, move the first task's work into a try and add CUSTOMER_TL.remove() in a finally. Run it again.

code.title: ScopedValueDemo.java (JDK 25)
code.html: // JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506), so no flag is needed. From labs/: // java vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.java // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where ScopedValue is a preview API. import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class ScopedValueDemo { static final ThreadLocal<String> CUSTOMER_TL = new ThreadLocal<>(); static final ScopedValue<String> CUSTOMER = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // deep in the call chain: reads the context, never sets it static String receiptLine() { return "ThreadLocal=" + CUSTOMER_TL.get() + ", ScopedValue=" + CUSTOMER.orElse("unbound"); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. a ThreadLocal set on a pooled thread and never removed try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { pool.submit(() -> { CUSTOMER_TL.set("ann"); // forgot CUSTOMER_TL.remove() return receiptLine(); }).get(); System.out.println("1. next task, same pool thread: " + pool.submit(ScopedValueDemo::receiptLine).get()); } // 2. a scoped value is bound for one call, and gone afterwards ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(() -> System.out.println("2. inside run(): " + receiptLine())); System.out.println(" after run(): " + receiptLine()); // 3. rebind for a nested call; the outer binding comes back when it returns ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(() -> { ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ben").run(() -> System.out.println("3. nested: " + receiptLine())); System.out.println(" outer again: " + receiptLine()); }); // 4. a thread you start yourself does not inherit the binding ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(() -> { Thread child = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("4. plain thread: " + receiptLine())); try { child.join(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } }

alt.title: ScopedValueDemo.kt (JDK 25)
alt.html: // JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506). Needs the Kotlin command-line // compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar // java -jar vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where ScopedValue is a preview API. import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val CUSTOMER_TL = ThreadLocal<String>() private val CUSTOMER: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() // deep in the call chain: reads the context, never sets it private fun receiptLine() = "ThreadLocal=${CUSTOMER_TL.get()}, ScopedValue=${CUSTOMER.orElse("unbound")}" fun main() { // 1. a ThreadLocal set on a pooled thread and never removed Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> pool.submit(Callable { CUSTOMER_TL.set("ann") // forgot CUSTOMER_TL.remove() receiptLine() }).get() println("1. next task, same pool thread: " + pool.submit(Callable { receiptLine() }).get()) } // 2. a scoped value is bound for one call, and gone afterwards // Runnable { } is optional; it shows this is the binding's run, not Kotlin's run {} ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(Runnable { println("2. inside run(): " + receiptLine()) }) println(" after run(): " + receiptLine()) // 3. rebind for a nested call; the outer binding comes back when it returns ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(Runnable { ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ben").run(Runnable { println("3. nested: " + receiptLine()) }) println(" outer again: " + receiptLine()) }) // 4. a thread you start yourself does not inherit the binding ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(Runnable { val child = Thread.ofVirtual().start { println("4. plain thread: " + receiptLine()) } child.join() }) }

try.expect: Line 1 shows ThreadLocal=ann in a task that never set it: the value leaked from the previous task on the same pool thread. After your fix it shows ThreadLocal=null. The scoped value is ann inside run() and unbound after it, ben in the nested call and ann again after it. The plain virtual thread prints unbound, because only StructuredTaskScope forks see the parent's binding. The Java and Kotlin versions print the same six lines.

compare.title: Request details that follow the subtasks

java.title: Java: ScopedValue plus a scope (JDK 25, scope in preview)
java.html: static final ScopedValue<String> CUSTOMER = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // final in JDK 25 Receipt checkout(Order order) throws Exception { return ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, order.customer()).call(() -> { // bound for this call try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // preview in JDK 25 Subtask<Approval> bank = scope.fork(() -> theBank.approve(order)); Subtask<String> line = scope.fork(() -> receiptLine(order.item())); scope.join(); return new Receipt(line.get(), bank.get()); } }); } static String receiptLine(String item) { return item + " for " + CUSTOMER.get(); // the fork reads the parent's binding }

kotlin.title: Kotlin: a coroutine context element
kotlin.html: // the coroutine carries the details, not the thread class Customer(val name: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(Customer) { companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<Customer> } suspend fun checkout(order: Order): Receipt = withContext(Customer(order.customer)) { // bound for this block val bank = async { theBank.approve(order) } val line = async { receiptLine(order.item) } // children inherit the context Receipt(line.await(), bank.await()) } suspend fun receiptLine(item: String): String = item + " for " + (currentCoroutineContext()[Customer]?.name ?: error("no customer"))

compare.note: Both are read-only details that children inherit and that end with the block. The difference is what carries them. A scoped value is bound to a thread's call stack, and only StructuredTaskScope forks inherit it. A coroutine context element is bound to the coroutine, so it survives when the coroutine moves to another thread at a suspension point, and every child started with launch or async inherits it. That's why scoped values and ThreadLocals are the wrong tool inside suspending code: a coroutine can resume on a different thread, where the binding isn't there. In Kotlin coroutine code, put the details in the coroutine context. Use ScopedValue from Kotlin only in plain blocking code on threads, as ScopedValueDemo.kt does.

worked.title: Make the order page fail fast

steps.say: The shop's order page needs two answers: the delivery date from the delivery company's web service (300 ms) and the customer's loyalty points (80 ms). Both are blocking calls. The code runs on a shared executor kept in a field, and the order id lives in a ThreadLocal for the log. Read it, and list what goes wrong when one call fails.
steps.code: OrderPage show(Order o) throws Exception { ORDER_ID.set(o.id()); // a ThreadLocal Future<LocalDate> date = shared.submit(() -> delivery.estimate(o)); // 300 ms Future<Integer> points = shared.submit(() -> loyalty.points(o)); // 80 ms return new OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()); }

alt.html: fun show(o: Order): OrderPage { ORDER_ID.set(o.id) // a ThreadLocal val date = shared.submit(Callable { delivery.estimate(o) }) // 300 ms val points = shared.submit(Callable { loyalty.points(o) }) // 80 ms return OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()) }

steps.say: Three problems. If the points call fails, date.get() still waits up to 300 ms first. If the delivery call fails, the points call keeps running after show has thrown. And both subtasks log without the order id, because ORDER_ID is set on the handler's thread only. On a pooled handler thread it is also never cleared.

On JDK 25 without preview, use a scope that owns its threads, like the lab's FailFastScope, and pass the order id as an argument. Every subtask now ends before show returns, and the first failure cancels the other call.
steps.code: OrderPage show(Order o) throws Exception { try (var scope = new FailFastScope()) { // 1. open: owns the subtasks String id = o.id(); // 2. details as a plain argument Supplier<LocalDate> date = scope.fork(() -> delivery.estimate(o, id)); Supplier<Integer> points = scope.fork(() -> loyalty.points(o, id)); scope.join(); // 3. first failure cancels the other return new OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()); } // 4. close: nothing left running }

alt.html: fun show(o: Order): OrderPage = FailFastScope().use { scope -> // 1. open: owns the subtasks val id = o.id // 2. details as a plain argument val date = scope.fork { delivery.estimate(o, id) } val points = scope.fork { loyalty.points(o, id) } scope.join() // 3. first failure cancels the other OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()) } // 4. close: nothing left running

steps.say: On JDK 25 with --enable-preview, the JDK's scope does the same job, and a scoped value carries the order id into both forks. No method signature has to change.
steps.code: static final ScopedValue<String> ORDER_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); OrderPage show(Order o) throws Exception { return ScopedValue.where(ORDER_ID, o.id()).call(() -> { // 1. bind the details try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // 2. fail-fast scope Subtask<LocalDate> date = scope.fork(() -> delivery.estimate(o)); // forks read ORDER_ID Subtask<Integer> points = scope.fork(() -> loyalty.points(o)); scope.join(); // 3. FailedException on JDK 25 return new OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()); } // 4. close: nothing left running }); }

alt.html: val ORDER_ID: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() fun show(o: Order): OrderPage = ScopedValue.where(ORDER_ID, o.id).call<OrderPage, Exception> { // 1. bind the details StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // 2. fail-fast scope val date = scope.fork(Callable { delivery.estimate(o) }) // forks read ORDER_ID val points = scope.fork(Callable { loyalty.points(o) }) scope.join() // 3. FailedException on JDK 25 OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()) } // 4. close: nothing left running }

steps.say: When you move to JDK 27 or 28, change the error handling where you call show: catch ExecutionException from join() instead of StructuredTaskScope.FailedException. The fork, join and close lines stay the same.

lab.title: Build a fail-fast scope on an executor
steps: Run the tests once. All seven fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Read the class comment in FailFastScope: it lists the rules the tests check.

Add the state as fields: an ExecutorService from Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), a CopyOnWriteArrayList<Future<?>>, an AtomicReference<Throwable> for the first failure and a volatile boolean joined.

Write fork. Submit a Callable that runs task.call() in a try. In the catch, record the failure with compareAndSet(null, failure), and if that wins, call executor.shutdownNow() to interrupt the siblings. Rethrow. Add the future to the list and return a Supplier that throws IllegalStateException until join() has run, then returns future.resultNow().
Handle a fork after a cancel: once the executor is shut down, submit throws RejectedExecutionException. Catch it and return a handle whose get() always throws IllegalStateException.

Write join: call get() on each future in order, ignore ExecutionException and CancellationException, and stop as soon as a failure is recorded. Set joined, then throw new ExecutionException(failure) if there was one. Write close: shutdownNow(), then close() on the executor.
Run the tests until all seven pass, then run them twice more.
hints: Why compareAndSet? The siblings you interrupt fail too, with InterruptedException. They fail after the real failure is recorded, so their compareAndSet(null, ...) returns false, and they don't replace it.

Don't cancel with future.cancel(true). A cancelled future counts as done at once, and on JDK 21 the executor then stops waiting for that thread while its finally block still runs. The close() test catches exactly that. shutdownNow() interrupts the threads and leaves the futures alone.
catch (Throwable failure) { ...; throw failure; } compiles inside the submitted lambda: Java's precise rethrow knows that task.call() can only throw an Exception.
Future.resultNow() (JDK 19 and later) returns the result of a task that succeeded, and throws IllegalStateException for one that failed or was cancelled, which is what a handle needs after join().
lab.done: All seven tests in FailFastScopeTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the JDK 25 scope from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Receipt checkout(Order order) that asks the bank and the stock service at the same time with StructuredTaskScope (JDK 25 preview), fails fast and closes cleanly. Then write the catch clause a caller needs on JDK 25, and the one it needs on JDK 27.

answer.html: Receipt checkout(Order order) throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // default: fail on the first failure Subtask<Approval> bank = scope.fork(() -> theBank.approve(order)); Subtask<Stock> stock = scope.fork(() -> stockService.check(order)); scope.join(); // throws if a subtask failed return new Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get()); // get() only after join() } // close() waits for every subtask } // a caller on JDK 25 try { return checkout(order); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.FailedException e) { // unchecked; the cause is the subtask's exception throw new CheckoutFailedException(e.getCause()); } // on JDK 27 and later, join() throws the checked ExecutionException instead: // } catch (ExecutionException e) { throw new CheckoutFailedException(e.getCause()); }

alt.html: fun checkout(order: Order): Receipt = StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // default: fail on the first failure val bank = scope.fork(Callable { theBank.approve(order) }) val stock = scope.fork(Callable { stockService.check(order) }) scope.join() // throws if a subtask failed Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get()) // get() only after join() } // close() waits for every subtask // a caller on JDK 25 try { return checkout(order) } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.FailedException) { // the cause is the subtask's exception throw CheckoutFailedException(e.cause) } // on JDK 27 and later, catch ExecutionException instead: // } catch (e: ExecutionException) { throw CheckoutFailedException(e.cause) }

recap: An executor fan-out doesn't cancel the other tasks when one fails, and with a shared executor they outlive the request.
Structured concurrency ties subtasks to a block: fork, join, and a close that guarantees every subtask has ended.
Fail fast means the first failure interrupts the siblings and join() throws it. Built by hand, close() must wait for the threads, not for the futures.
The limit: StructuredTaskScope is a preview in JDK 25 to 27 and needs --enable-preview (open(), a Joiner and FailedException in 25, ExecutionException from 27). JDK 28 makes it final.
Scoped values are final in JDK 25: bound for one call with where(...).run(...), read-only, gone afterwards, and inherited only by StructuredTaskScope forks.
A ThreadLocal used for a request's details can be changed by anyone, leaks on pooled threads without remove(), and is copied by InheritableThreadLocal.

explain.prompt: A colleague says that try-with-resources around newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() already gives you structured concurrency. Explain what it gives you, what it is missing, and what StructuredTaskScope and scoped values add.
explain.answer: It gives you half of it. When the block ends, close() waits for every task, so no task outlives the method. What it lacks is a failure policy: when one task fails, nothing cancels the others, so a failed checkout still waits for the slowest call, and you must write cancel calls on every error path yourself. Hand-made cancelling also has traps, such as close() not waiting for a task you cancelled with cancel(true). StructuredTaskScope adds the policy (the first failure cancels the siblings, or another Joiner, such as first success wins), timeouts and checks that scopes nest properly, and its close() always waits for the threads. It's still a preview until JDK 28. Scoped values, final in JDK 25, add request details that flow into the scope's subtasks without copying, that called code can't change, and that disappear when the call ends, unlike a ThreadLocal.

deeper.html:
Joiners of your own. A Joiner has two hooks, onFork and onComplete, and a result() method that join() calls at the end. onComplete returns true to cancel the scope. That's enough for policies the built-in joiners don't cover, such as "stop once three of five price services agree" or "collect the successes and ignore the failures". onComplete runs on the thread of the subtask that just finished, so a joiner's state must be thread-safe. Check the Javadoc of the exact JDK you use, because JDK 26 changed the hook signatures slightly.

Why CompletableFuture doesn't solve this. allOf waits for everything even after one future fails, and cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture doesn't interrupt the thread doing the work: it only completes the future. The lesson "CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out" builds a fan-out that way. Notice how much code its error handling needs compared with a scope.

Kotlin already has this. In coroutine code, coroutineScope { async { } } gives the same guarantees without a preview flag: children can't outlive the scope, the first failure cancels the siblings, and cancelling reaches each child at its next suspension point. The coroutines track covers it. StructuredTaskScope matters most for Java code, and for Kotlin code that blocks on threads.

Scoped values and virtual threads. A ThreadLocal costs a map entry per thread, and with a million virtual threads that adds up, as lesson 4 of this track showed. A scoped value's binding belongs to the call, not to each thread, and the scope's forks share it. That makes it a natural fit for one virtual thread per request with many short subtasks.

Old articles. Before JDK 25 the API was StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure and ShutdownOnSuccess, subclasses you created with new. Scoped values had static helpers such as ScopedValue.runWhere, which were removed during the previews. If a snippet uses either, it was written for an older preview.
